title: Mingus's writing: "Porkpie Hat" and why not to write the unplayable
summary: Callender argues for writing music people can play rather than extending players to their limit.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, Gerald, being the kind of very outspoken person that he is, pulls no punches about anybody. Either he liked it or he didn't. Well, Gerald didn't have too much respect for him. That's just the way it goes. So he developed into a writer who may or may not have been way ahead of his time. Because his object in music was to astound everybody, and so he would write things... He'd

figure them out in his head, and I'd look at them... I was showing my wife one of the things he wrote, "Porkpie Hat." He had written it so that it was very difficult, and I showed her how it could have been simplified -- and she got the message. Because it's easy to write stuff that nobody can play. You know what I mean?

He'd get very angry if people didn't play it the way he'd conceived it in his head. But upon analyzing some of it, I can see, "Hey, he could have done this a lot simpler" -- which is my premise in music. I've always figured that if I write things that people can play, they're going to play it and it will sound better, and I don't want to extent everybody to the limit of their ability every time. Because a note happens to be playable on an instrument, it doesn't make it always practical to write it. Does that make sense?

For instance, trumpets can play up to altimissimo G, which is Miles above the staff. But you don't write them up there all the time because it's hard to play. I found...when I used to first write music... We're still talking about Mingus, but I'm sidetracking.
